info.name: Library 3-tier (Day 4)
info.description:
Every endpoint of `library-web-service`, ready to click.

The service runs on port 8080 and all paths start with `/api`.
Start it from the TOP folder of the project:

    mvn install -DskipTests
    mvn -pl library-web-service spring-boot:run

### How the folders work

The project changes shape while you work on it, so the same endpoint needs two
different request bodies at two different times.

- **Folder 1** is the shape the service speaks **today**, before you write the DTO.
  A book carries a nested `category` object.
- **Folder 2** is the shape it speaks **after steps 2 to 5**.
  A book is flat: `category_id` and `category_name`, no nesting.

Run folder 1 first and look at the JSON. Then do the steps, then run folder 2.
Seeing the same endpoint answer differently is the whole lesson.

### Variables

`baseUrl` is `http://localhost:8080/api`. Change it in one place if your port differs.
`bookId` is 10002 ("1984") - a book that `data.sql` always creates.
`newBookId` fills itself in after you create a book, so DELETE has something to delete.

### One thing Postman cannot show you

CORS. Only a browser enforces it, so step 7 looks fine from here even when it is
broken. "It works in Postman" proves nothing about the web page.

item.name: 0. Is the service up?
item.description: Run these two first. They touch no database and no DTO, so if they answer, the service itself is healthy.

request.description:
The smallest possible endpoint.
Answers the plain text `Hi There!`.

If this fails, nothing else in the collection will work. Check that
`spring-boot:run` is still going and that MySQL is running.

Shows a path variable.
The `Somchai` part of the URL arrives in the method as `@PathVariable String name`.

Change the name in the URL and send it again.

item.name: 1. Books - before the DTO (entity shape)
item.description:
The service as it is on day 4 morning: the `Book` entity goes straight out as JSON.

Look at what comes back. Every book drags a whole nested `category` object with it,
including a description nobody asked for. That is the problem the DTO solves.

request.description:
`GET /api/books` - the ten books from `data.sql`.

Read one entry closely:

    {"id":10002,"title":"1984","author":"George Orwell",
     "addedDate":"15-01-2026",
     "category":{"id":10002,"name":"Science Fiction","description":"..."},
     "publish-year":1949}

Nested, and mixed naming: `addedDate` in camelCase but `publish-year` with a minus
sign, because the entity carries a `@JsonProperty`. The DTO will make all of it
consistent.

`GET /api/books/10002` - "1984".

Keep this response open in a second tab. After step 4 you will send the exact same
request and the answer will look different.

item.name: Get a book that does not exist (404)

request.description:
There is no book 999999, so the controller answers **404 Not Found** with an empty body.

An API says "I could not find it" with a status code, not with an error message in a
200 response. Check the status at the top of the response pane.

`GET /api/books/title/the` - every book whose title contains "the", ignoring case.

The repository method is `findByTitleContainingIgnoreCase`. Spring Data wrote the
query from that name alone.

Try `gatsby`, or `THE`, and watch the SQL appear in the terminal running the service.

`GET /api/books/year/1949` - the books published that year.

`data.sql` has books from 1813, 1925, 1932, 1937, 1949, 1951, 1953, 1960, 1967 and 1987.
An empty list `[]` is a correct answer for any other year - not an error.

exec: // Remembers the id of the book you just created, so the DELETE
// request below has something to delete.
// The response is plain text before step 4 and JSON after it,

request.description:
`POST /api/books` - answers **201 Created**.

This is the body the service needs **today**, and it is awkward:

    "category": { "id": 10002 }

The client has to know the entity's inner shape and wrap one number in an object.
After step 4 the same request becomes `"category_id": 10002` - see folder 2.

Three things to notice:

- `Content-Type: application/json` is required. Without it Spring answers
  **415 Unsupported Media Type**.
- The date is `dd-MM-yyyy`, because `LocalDateDeserializer` says so.
  `2026-07-30` will fail.
- Do not send an `id`. Hibernate generates it.

The answer is a **sentence**, not JSON: `Book created with ID: 11`. That is the
method returning `ResponseEntity<String>`. Step 4 changes it to return the saved
book as a DTO, which is what a REST client actually wants.

item.name: Create a book with a bad category (400)

request.description:
Category 999999 does not exist, so the controller answers **400 Bad Request** and
saves nothing.

The category must already exist in this project - creating a book does not create
its category. In `lab-web-3tier` it is the other way round, because the lab uses
`@ManyToOne(cascade = CascadeType.ALL)`.

`DELETE /api/books/{id}` - **200 OK**, or **404** if that id is gone already.

`{{newBookId}}` was filled in by the create request above, so run that one first.

Deleting one of the ten seeded books is safe too. `ddl-auto=create-drop` rebuilds
the tables and re-runs `data.sql` every time the service restarts.

item.name: 2. Books - after the DTO (steps 2 to 5)
item.description:
Run this folder **after** you finish steps 2, 3, 4 and 5.

Before that, the DTO requests fail in a way that is worth seeing once:
the body you send does not fit the entity, so nothing you sent arrives.

request.description:
The same URL as in folder 1. Compare the two answers side by side.

    {"id":10002,"title":"1984","author":"George Orwell",
     "publish-year":1949,"added-date":"15-01-2026",
     "category_id":10002,"category_name":"Science Fiction"}

Flat. Consistently named. No `description`.
And the client still learns the category name without a second request - that is
the "reduce the number of calls" argument for a DTO.

No `transactions` list either, because `BookDTO` has no such field. The DTO decides
what travels.

Ten flat books.

This is the response the web page reads in step 8. It uses the DTO's JSON names,
so in jQuery you write `book['publish-year']` and `book.category_name` - not
`book.year` and not `book.category.name`.

The same book as in folder 1, with the body a client would rather write:
one flat `category_id` instead of a nested object.

Answers **201 Created**, and the body is now the saved book as a DTO - with the
id the database gave it.

This is the request `testCreateAcceptsTheDtoShape` in `BookResourceIT` sends.

**The point of the whole session.** Step 5.

One field goes in. Everything else must survive:

    {"id":10002,"title":"1984 (revised)","author":"George Orwell",
     "publish-year":1949,"added-date":"15-01-2026",
     "category_id":10002,"category_name":"Science Fiction"}

It survives because the controller **loads the existing book first** and the mapper
only copies fields that are not null. That `if (dto.getTitle() != null)` in the
generated `BookMapperImpl` is the entire feature.

If the author, year and date come back `null`, it is one of two things:
`@BeanMapping(nullValuePropertyMappingStrategy = IGNORE)` is missing, or a `BookDTO`
field is `int` instead of `Integer`. Go back to step 2.

Now send it a second time. Same answer - a PATCH is safe to repeat.

item.name: PATCH a book that does not exist (404)

request.description:
**404 Not Found**, because step 1 of the PATCH recipe is `findById` and answer 404
if it is absent.

A PATCH must never create a row. If this returns 200 or 500, the `isPresent()` check
is missing.

This is `testPatchUnknownBookIs404`.

item.name: PUT - the same body, the opposite result

request.description:
Optional, and only works if you also write a `updateBook` method that builds a
`new Book()` instead of loading the existing one. Otherwise Postman shows
**405 Method Not Allowed** - which itself tells you the URL exists but the verb
does not.

With PUT written that way, the same one-field body wipes the rest:

    {"title":"1984 (replaced)","author":null,"publish-year":null,
     "added-date":null,"category_name":null}

Same body, opposite outcome. **PATCH merges, PUT replaces.**
That difference is the reason an API needs both verbs.

Restart the service to get "1984" back.

item.name: 3. Transactions
item.description:
Borrowing and returning. This controller has no DTO today - it is the "before"
picture, left in on purpose so you can see what the book endpoints used to look like.

request.description:
`POST /api/transactions` - **201 Created**.

Member 1 is Alice Johnson; `data.sql` creates members 1 to 10.
`type` is `BORROW` or `RETURN`.

Do not send `transactionDate`. The controller sets it to today, server-side.
A date the client can choose is a date the client can lie about.

Two nested objects here, for the same reason the old book POST had one. Writing
`TransactionDTO` with a flat `member_id` and `book_id` is the exercise if you want
to prove the pattern repeats - the solution branch already has it.

The same request with a different `type`.

Nothing stops a RETURN without a BORROW. The rule "you can only return what you
borrowed" is business logic, and no controller here checks it yet.

**400 Bad Request** - `Member not found with ID: 999999`.

The controller checks the member and the book before saving anything. Both must
exist.

Empty on a fresh start, because `data.sql` seeds no transactions. Create one above
first.

Look at how much JSON one transaction produces: the whole book, the whole category
inside it, and the whole member. Three tables in one response, and the client
probably wanted two names and a date.

That is the argument for a DTO, stated in bytes.
